subject: Physics
title: Electricity & Circuits Lab
summary: Build circuits on a breadboard: see how current, voltage and resistance fit together, how two bulbs behave in series and in parallel, and why a thin wire makes a good fuse. Predict first, then watch what really happens.

scenarios.title: The Ohm's Law Bench
scenarios.setup: A battery, a resistor and an ammeter on a breadboard. Slide the voltage and change the resistance: a V–I graph plots every reading.

trials.prompt: The resistor is 4 Ω. At 2 V the ammeter reads 0.5 A. You slide the battery up to 4 V and keep the resistor the same. What will the ammeter read?
trials.outcome: 1 A: twice the 0.5 A. Every reading lands on one straight line through the origin of the V–I graph.
trials.explanation: For the same resistor, current is directly proportional to voltage: I = V ÷ R. Change the voltage by a factor and the current changes by the same factor, so the V–I points make a straight line through the origin.

trials.prompt: The battery is 4 V and the resistor is 4 Ω: the ammeter reads 1 A. You keep the voltage the same and swap in a resistor of 8 Ω. What happens to the current?
trials.outcome: The current becomes 0.5 A: more resistance, less current.
trials.explanation: I = V ÷ R. With the voltage fixed, current is inversely proportional to resistance: resistance opposes the flow, so raising it lowers the current. Here 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5 A. It is a common slip to think more resistance means more current.

trials.prompt: The V–I graph of a resistor is a straight line through the origin, and it passes through the point I = 0.6 A, V = 6 V. What is the resistance of the resistor?
trials.explanation: On a V–I graph the slope is V ÷ I, which is the resistance: 6 V ÷ 0.6 A = 10 Ω.

variants.prompt: The V–I graph for a resistor is a straight line through the origin. Which quantity does its slope give?
variants.explanation: The slope is the change in voltage divided by the change in current. By Ohm's law V ÷ I is the resistance, and for an ohmic resistor it is the same everywhere on the line.

variants.prompt: A short thick wire and a long thin wire of the same metal are connected to the same battery in turn. Which carries more current?

variants.prompt: A circuit carries 2 A. The resistance triples and the battery stays the same. What is the current now?
variants.explanation: I = V ÷ R, so with three times the resistance the current is a third: 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67 A.

scenarios.title: The Bulb Bench
scenarios.setup: Two identical bulbs and a battery on a breadboard, with a single bulb alongside for comparison. Wire the two bulbs in series or in parallel, and unscrew one.

trials.prompt: Two identical 6 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 6 V battery. Compared with one bulb alone across the same battery, how bright is each of the two?
trials.outcome: Each bulb is dimmer: about a quarter as bright as the single bulb.
trials.explanation: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each gets half of it. Half the voltage gives half the current, and brightness depends on the power, which falls to a quarter.

variants.prompt: Two identical 6 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 6 V battery. Compared with one bulb alone across the same battery, how bright is each of the two?
variants.outcome: Each bulb is dimmer: about a quarter as bright as the single bulb.
variants.explanation: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each gets half of it. Half the voltage gives half the current, and brightness depends on the power, which falls to a quarter.

variants.prompt: Two identical 6 Ω bulbs are wired in parallel across a 6 V battery. Compared with one bulb alone across the same battery, how bright is each of the two?
variants.outcome: Each bulb is just as bright as the single bulb.
variants.explanation: In parallel each bulb is connected straight across the battery, so each gets the full voltage and draws the same current as a single bulb would. The battery simply supplies twice the current.

variants.prompt: You have two identical 4 Ω bulbs and a 9 V battery. In which wiring will the bulbs be brighter?
variants.outcome: Brighter in parallel: full battery voltage across each bulb, instead of half.
variants.explanation: Each bulb gets the full battery voltage in parallel but only half in series, so parallel bulbs carry twice the current of series bulbs and are four times as bright.

variants.prompt: A 6 V battery drives 2 A through one 3 Ω bulb. Two identical bulbs are now wired in series with the battery. What current does the battery supply?
variants.outcome: 1 A: half. The total resistance has doubled.
variants.explanation: In series the resistances add, so two bulbs have twice the resistance of one. For the same battery, I = V ÷ R, so the current is halved.

variants.prompt: A 12 V battery drives 2 A through one 6 Ω bulb. Two identical bulbs are now wired in parallel across the battery. What current does the battery supply?
variants.outcome: 4 A: twice as much. Each bulb draws its own current.
variants.explanation: Each parallel branch draws its own current straight from the battery, so the battery supplies the sum of the two: twice the current of one bulb.

trials.prompt: The two bulbs are in series and both are lit. You unscrew bulb 2. What happens to bulb 1?

options.label: It stays lit just as bright

trials.outcome: Bulb 1 goes out too, and the ammeter reads zero.
trials.explanation: A series circuit has only one path for the current. Taking out any bulb breaks that path, so the current stops everywhere and both bulbs go out.

variants.prompt: The two bulbs are in series and both are lit. You unscrew bulb 2. What happens to bulb 1?

options.label: It stays lit just as bright

variants.outcome: Bulb 1 goes out too, and the ammeter reads zero.
variants.explanation: A series circuit has only one path for the current. Taking out any bulb breaks that path, so the current stops everywhere and both bulbs go out.

variants.prompt: The two bulbs are in parallel and both are lit. You unscrew bulb 2. What happens to bulb 1?

options.label: It stays lit just as bright

variants.outcome: Bulb 1 stays lit, just as bright as before.
variants.explanation: Each parallel branch has its own path from the battery. Removing one bulb opens only its own branch; the other still has the full battery voltage and the same current.

variants.prompt: The two bulbs are in series and both are lit. You unscrew bulb 1. What happens to bulb 2?

options.label: It stays lit just as bright

variants.outcome: Bulb 2 goes out too, and the ammeter reads zero.
variants.explanation: A series circuit has only one path for the current. Taking out any bulb breaks that path, so the current stops everywhere and both bulbs go out.

variants.prompt: The two bulbs are in parallel and both are lit. You unscrew bulb 1. What happens to bulb 2?

options.label: It stays lit just as bright

variants.outcome: Bulb 2 stays lit, just as bright as before.
variants.explanation: Each parallel branch has its own path from the battery. Removing one bulb opens only its own branch; the other still has the full battery voltage and the same current.

variants.prompt: The two bulbs are in parallel and the ammeter in the battery lead reads 2 A. You unscrew bulb 2. What does the ammeter read now?
variants.outcome: 1 A: half. Only one branch is left drawing current.
variants.explanation: Each branch draws its own current. With one branch removed the battery supplies only the remaining branch's current: half the total.

trials.prompt: Two identical 4 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 12 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
trials.explanation: In series the resistances add: 2 × 4 = 8 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.

variants.prompt: Two identical 4 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 12 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
variants.explanation: In series the resistances add: 2 × 4 = 8 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.

variants.prompt: Two identical 3 Ω bulbs are wired in parallel across a 6 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
variants.explanation: Each parallel bulb draws 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A and the battery supplies both: 2 × 2 = 4 A.

variants.prompt: Two identical 6 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 9 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
variants.explanation: In series the resistances add: 2 × 6 = 12 Ω, so I = 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A.

variants.prompt: Two identical 8 Ω bulbs are wired in parallel across a 12 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
variants.explanation: Each parallel bulb draws 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A and the battery supplies both: 2 × 1.5 = 3 A.

variants.prompt: Two identical 1.5 Ω bulbs are wired in series across a 6 V battery, with an ammeter in the battery lead. Predict its reading.
variants.explanation: In series the resistances add: 2 × 1.5 = 3 Ω, so I = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A.

trials.prompt: Why are the lights in a house wired in parallel rather than in series?

options.label: Each light works on its own, and each gets the full voltage
So that they are all dimmer and save energy
Because there is only one wire to the house

trials.outcome: Each light works on its own, and each gets the full voltage.
trials.explanation: In parallel each lamp has its own path from the supply, so switching one off or a bulb failing does not stop the rest, and each gets the full voltage.

variants.prompt: Why are the lights in a house wired in parallel rather than in series?

options.label: Each light works on its own, and each gets the full voltage
So that they are all dimmer and save energy
Because there is only one wire to the house

variants.outcome: Each light works on its own, and each gets the full voltage.
variants.explanation: In parallel each lamp has its own path from the supply, so switching one off or a bulb failing does not stop the rest, and each gets the full voltage.

variants.prompt: A string of old Christmas-tree lights is wired in series. One bulb blows. What happens?
variants.explanation: A blown bulb breaks the only path for the current, so every bulb in the series string goes out.

variants.prompt: An ammeter measures the current in a circuit. How must it be connected?

options.label: In series with the part you are measuring
In parallel across the part you are measuring

variants.outcome: In series with the part you are measuring.
variants.explanation: The ammeter must carry the same current as the component, so it goes in the same loop: in series. It has a very low resistance so it hardly changes the current.

variants.prompt: A voltmeter measures the voltage across a bulb. How must it be connected?
variants.explanation: A voltmeter compares the two ends of a component, so it is connected across it, in parallel. It has a very high resistance so it takes almost no current.

variants.prompt: Two identical resistors are connected in parallel. Compared with one of them, the total resistance is…
variants.explanation: Two equal parallel paths let twice the current flow for the same voltage, so the total resistance is half of one.

scenarios.title: The Fuse Bench
scenarios.setup: A thin fuse wire in series with a resistor and a variable voltage source, with thick copper leads and an ammeter. Raise the voltage slowly and watch the wire.

trials.prompt: A thin fuse wire rated for 2 A is in series with a 4.5 Ω resistor. You slowly raise the voltage of the supply. What happens to the fuse wire?

options.label: It glows red, then melts and breaks the circuit
It glows but never melts, however high the voltage

trials.outcome: It glows, then melts at about 10 V when the current reaches 2 A, and the circuit breaks.
trials.explanation: A current heats the wire it flows through. The thin fuse wire has the most resistance, so it heats the most. When the current reaches its rating the wire melts and breaks the circuit, which cuts off the current.

variants.prompt: A thin fuse wire rated for 2 A is in series with a 4.5 Ω resistor. You slowly raise the voltage of the supply. What happens to the fuse wire?

options.label: It glows red, then melts and breaks the circuit
It glows but never melts, however high the voltage

variants.outcome: It glows, then melts at about 10 V when the current reaches 2 A, and the circuit breaks.
variants.explanation: A current heats the wire it flows through. The thin fuse wire has the most resistance, so it heats the most. When the current reaches its rating the wire melts and breaks the circuit, which cuts off the current.

variants.prompt: A thin fuse wire rated for 3 A is in series with a 5.5 Ω resistor and an ammeter. The voltage is raised until the wire melts. What does the ammeter read afterwards?
variants.outcome: Zero: the gap in the wire breaks the circuit.
variants.explanation: Once the wire has melted there is a gap in the only path, so no current can flow at all. That is how a fuse protects the rest of the circuit.

variants.prompt: The current through the fuse wire is doubled, for the same length of time. What happens to the heat produced in the wire?

options.label: It becomes four times as much

variants.explanation: The heat produced is H = I²Rt. The current is squared, so twice the current gives four times the heat.

variants.prompt: The fuse is rated for 4 A. The voltage is raised until the circuit tries to carry 6 A through it. What happens?

options.label: The wire melts and the circuit breaks
The wire gets longer but keeps conducting

variants.outcome: The wire melts and the circuit breaks.
variants.explanation: A fuse wire is made to melt when the current goes above its rating. At 1.5 times the rating the heating, which goes as I², is more than twice as much, so it melts.

variants.prompt: A 5 A fuse wire is in series with a 3.5 Ω resistor. Which part of the circuit warms up most as the current rises?

options.label: They all warm up the same

variants.explanation: The same current flows through everything in the loop, but heat is I²Rt: the thin fuse wire has far more resistance than the thick leads, so it gets far hotter.

trials.prompt: A 2 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 4.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
trials.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 2 A. The total resistance is 4.5 + 0.5 = 5 Ω, so V = I R = 2 × 5 = 10 V.

variants.prompt: A 2 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 4.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
variants.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 2 A. The total resistance is 4.5 + 0.5 = 5 Ω, so V = I R = 2 × 5 = 10 V.

variants.prompt: A 3 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 5.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
variants.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 3 A. The total resistance is 5.5 + 0.5 = 6 Ω, so V = I R = 3 × 6 = 18 V.

variants.prompt: A 1 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 9.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
variants.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 1 A. The total resistance is 9.5 + 0.5 = 10 Ω, so V = I R = 1 × 10 = 10 V.

variants.prompt: A 5 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 3.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
variants.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 5 A. The total resistance is 3.5 + 0.5 = 4 Ω, so V = I R = 5 × 4 = 20 V.

variants.prompt: A 4 A fuse wire of resistance 0.5 Ω is in series with a 7.5 Ω resistor. At what supply voltage will the fuse just blow?
variants.explanation: The fuse blows when the current reaches 4 A. The total resistance is 7.5 + 0.5 = 8 Ω, so V = I R = 4 × 8 = 32 V.

trials.prompt: The same current flows through the thin 2 A fuse wire and through the thick copper leads beside it. As the voltage rises, which one melts first?
trials.outcome: The thin fuse wire melts; the thick leads stay cool.
trials.explanation: It is the same current in all of them, yet only the fuse wire melts. Heat is I²Rt: the thin wire has much more resistance than the thick leads, so it turns far more of the electrical energy into heat.

variants.prompt: The same current flows through the thin 2 A fuse wire and through the thick copper leads beside it. As the voltage rises, which one melts first?
variants.outcome: The thin fuse wire melts; the thick leads stay cool.
variants.explanation: It is the same current in all of them, yet only the fuse wire melts. Heat is I²Rt: the thin wire has much more resistance than the thick leads, so it turns far more of the electrical energy into heat.

variants.prompt: Someone replaces the thin 3 A fuse wire with a thick copper wire to stop it blowing. The voltage is raised well past the old limit. What happens to the thick wire?

options.label: It stays cool and keeps carrying the current, so the circuit is no longer protected
It melts at exactly the same current as the fuse wire

variants.outcome: The thick wire stays cool: nothing breaks the circuit any more.
variants.explanation: A thick wire has very little resistance, so the same current heats it far less (H = I²Rt) and it does not melt. Then nothing cuts off a dangerous current, which is why a fuse must never be replaced with a thicker wire.

variants.prompt: The fuse wire and a thick copper lead carry the same 5 A. The fuse wire's resistance is 50 times the lead's. How does the heat made each second in the fuse wire compare with the lead?
variants.explanation: For the same current, H = I²Rt is proportional to the resistance, so a wire with 50 times the resistance makes 50 times the heat each second.

variants.prompt: A heater's element is made of a thin, high-resistance wire, while the cable that brings the current to it is thick copper. Both carry the same current. Which gets glowing hot?
variants.outcome: The thin element glows hot; the cable stays cool.
variants.explanation: Same current, but H = I²Rt: the element has far more resistance, so nearly all the heat is made there and the cable stays cool.

variants.prompt: Two fuse wires carry the same current. Wire A is thin, wire B is thick. As the current rises towards 4 A, which one reaches melting first?
variants.explanation: The thin wire has the higher resistance, so it makes more heat for the same current (H = I²Rt) and reaches its melting point first.

trials.prompt: A plug has a 13 A fuse. An appliance develops a fault and tries to draw 40 A. What does the fuse do?

options.label: It melts and breaks the circuit
It makes the current smaller but keeps it flowing

trials.outcome: It melts and breaks the circuit.
trials.explanation: The fuse wire is designed to melt when the current is above its rating, which stops the flow before the cables overheat.

variants.prompt: A plug has a 13 A fuse. An appliance develops a fault and tries to draw 40 A. What does the fuse do?

options.label: It melts and breaks the circuit
It makes the current smaller but keeps it flowing

variants.outcome: It melts and breaks the circuit.
variants.explanation: The fuse wire is designed to melt when the current is above its rating, which stops the flow before the cables overheat.

variants.prompt: A toaster draws 3 A. Which fuse should it have?
variants.explanation: The fuse must be just above the normal current, so it lets the toaster work but blows if the current becomes too large. A 1 A fuse would blow at once, a 30 A fuse would not protect it.

variants.prompt: In which wire of an appliance cable is the fuse placed, and how?

options.label: In the live wire, in series with the appliance
Across the live and neutral wires, in parallel

variants.outcome: In the live wire, in series with the appliance.
variants.explanation: The fuse must carry the whole current of the appliance so it must be in series, and in the live wire so the appliance is cut off from the live supply when it blows.

variants.prompt: An electric kettle's element gets hot but its cable does not. Why?

options.label: The element has much more resistance, so the same current makes more heat in it
Less current flows in the cable
The cable has no resistance at all

variants.outcome: The element has much more resistance, so the same current makes more heat in it.
variants.explanation: The same current flows through both. H = I²Rt, so the part with the higher resistance makes far more heat.

variants.prompt: The current through a heater doubles. By how much does the heat it makes each second increase?
variants.explanation: H = I²Rt: heat grows with the square of the current.

laws.name: Ohm's law
laws.summary: For a resistor, current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.

laws.name: Series and parallel
laws.summary: Series circuits have one path; parallel circuits give each part its own path.

laws.name: Heating effect
laws.summary: A current heats the wire it flows through, most where the resistance is highest.
